title: Vector search
summary: How text becomes vectors, how a search finds the closest ones, and why fast indexes trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed.

blocks.p: A user types "can I get my money back?". The help article that answers it is titled "Refund policy" and never uses the word money. Keyword search, which matches words, misses it.
We want search by meaning. And with millions of documents, it has to answer in milliseconds.

An **embedding model** turns a piece of text into a **vector**: a list of numbers, often several hundred to a few thousand long. The model is trained so that texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions.

To search, embed every document once and store the vectors. At query time, embed the query and find the stored vectors closest to it. Closeness is usually measured by **cosine similarity**, the angle between two vectors, or by straight-line distance.
The figures here draw vectors in two dimensions so you can see them. Real ones have hundreds of dimensions, but the idea is the same.

blocks.h3: Exact search is slow at scale

blocks.p: The simplest search compares the query with every stored vector and keeps the closest. It always finds the true nearest neighbours. But the work grows with the number of vectors: a million vectors means a million comparisons for every query.

An **approximate nearest neighbour** (ANN) index looks at only part of the data. One common kind, **IVF**, groups the vectors into clusters ahead of time. A query is compared with each cluster's centre, then only with the vectors in the nearest few clusters.

blocks.caption: Exact search compares the query with all 88 vectors. IVF compares it with 4 cluster centres, then searches only the nearest cluster. It is much faster, but misses a neighbour that sits just over the border in Billing.

blocks.p: Searching more clusters finds more of the true neighbours and costs more time. The share of true neighbours found is called **recall**. Every ANN index has a setting that trades recall for speed.

Another common index, **HNSW**, links each vector to a few near neighbours in a layered graph. A search starts at the top layer and walks the graph toward the query. It is fast and accurate, and uses extra memory for the links.

blocks.caption: Memory to hold the raw vectors, before any index. Each number is a 4-byte float.

list: **Postgres can do this.** The [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) extension stores vectors in a table. It does exact search by default, and offers HNSW and IVFFlat indexes for approximate search.
**HNSW is the common default.** Malkov and Yashunin describe it in [their 2016 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320). Many vector databases use it.
**FAISS is the reference library.** Meta's [FAISS](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) implements exact search, IVF, HNSW and compression, on CPU and GPU.
**Measure recall on your data.** Build a set of queries, find their true neighbours with exact search, and check what the index returns. Tune it until recall is good enough for your use.
**Combine with keywords.** Vectors are weak on exact terms such as product codes or names. Many systems run keyword and vector search together and merge the results.
An embedding model turns text into a vector, and similar meanings land close together.
Search embeds the query and finds the nearest stored vectors.
Exact search compares against everything. Approximate indexes such as IVF and HNSW look at a fraction of the data.
Approximate search trades recall for speed, so measure recall on your own queries.
